title: Burial facing the qiblah
hook: quickly, facing the qiblah, in the earth

segments.voice: Yesterday, the funeral prayer, said standing, with no bowing and no prostration. Your line: stand for them. Did you think of someone you'd stand for? Today, the walk from the prayer to the grave. Day one thousand three hundred forty-two.

There is a burial in the Qur'an that begins in the worst way. In surah al-Ma'idah, one of Adam's two sons has killed his brother, and he stands there with the body and no idea what to do with it. Then Allah sends a raven. The bird scratches at the ground, digging, and the killer watches. He understands, and he's ashamed: he cries out, in paraphrase, that he couldn't even manage what this raven manages, to cover his brother. So a grave in the Qur'an is dug by someone learning from a bird. Today, the grave itself: which way the body faces, and why it's done quickly.
screen: `A BODY, AND NO IDEA WHAT TO DO.` → `A RAVEN SCRATCHES THE GROUND.` → `A GRAVE, LEARNED FROM A BIRD.`

segments.voice: Start with the speed. In Sahih al-Bukhari, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, tells people to hurry with the funeral. His reasoning, in paraphrase: if the one who died was good, you're bringing them toward good; if not, it's a weight you set down from your shoulders. So the washing, the shroud and the prayer you've met these last days are meant to come quickly, and the burial follows close behind. Grief doesn't get to wait for everything to be perfect. Then the direction. Every day of a Muslim's life, the prayer has faced one place: the qiblah, toward the Ka'bah in Makkah. In the grave, as the jurists describe it, the body is laid on its right side, the face turned toward that same direction. The one who stood in prayer facing the qiblah now lies facing it. A whole life of turning one way, and it doesn't stop at the end. And then the earth. Muslim burial is in the ground itself, plainly, in the white shroud. Mourners may help fill the grave by hand. And in surah Ta Ha, there's a verse some communities recite at that moment, in Pickthall's translation: "Thereof We created you, and thereunto We return you, and thence We bring you forth a second time." Three movements in one line. From the earth. Back to the earth. Out of it again. That's the shape this verse gives a burial: not a disappearance, but a return, with a promise folded inside it. In the verse, the ground isn't the end of the sentence. It's the comma.
screen: `HURRY WITH THE FUNERAL.` · `FACING THE QIBLAH, EVEN NOW.` · `INTO THE EARTH, BY HAND.` · `FROM IT, TO IT, OUT OF IT AGAIN.`

segments.voice: The practice: think of the earth. Sit, and let your weight settle down into the chair or the floor, and notice the ground holding you up. It's held you every day of your life without being asked. Breathe slowly. Bring to mind the soil somewhere you know: a garden, a park, a field you've walked through. What grows in it. What's under it. Hold the line from Ta Ha for a breath or two: from it, back to it, out of it again. If you pray, you can remember someone who has already been returned to the earth. The bell holds the time.
Burial facing the qiblah. The body laid in the earth, on its right side, facing the same direction it faced in prayer, and done without delay. Today's word.
Your line: back to the earth. Today, put your hand on real ground once, soil or grass, and leave it there for a breath. Tomorrow, three days. Day one thousand three hundred forty-two.

howItsDone: Muslims bury the dead soon after death, in the earth, wrapped in the shroud and laid on the right side facing the qiblah; mourners help fill the grave, and some communities recite Qur'an 20:55 as they do.

fork.setup: you're Adam's son, standing with your brother's body. a raven lands and starts to dig. what do you do?
options: watch, and learn to cover him.
fork.reveal: in al-Ma'idah he watches the raven and learns, and cries out in shame that a bird knew more than he did.

original.note: Arabic: the direction faced in prayer, toward the Ka'bah.

trapdoor: what you thought: a Muslim burial is just a quiet, quick funeral.
what it means: the body goes into the earth soon, in the shroud, turned toward the qiblah it faced in every prayer.
what a scholar hears: Ta Ha 20:55, from the earth, to it, and out again, and al-Bukhari's hadith on hurrying the bier.

notes: Editor: hook no longer promises 'how it's dug' (the teach doesn't say); softened 'often happen fast' and 'often by hand' to unsourced-claim-safe wording; tied the closing 'comma' line to the verse rather than the narrator.
Bukhari 1315 paraphrased; confirm number and wording.
Laying on the right side facing the qiblah is stated as the jurists' description; confirm phrasing and whether to cite a specific text.
'Some communities recite 20:55' while filling the grave: confirm this is fair to say.
The hook avoids calling this the first burial; tradition often says so, but the verse does not.
